paras.text: Halogens in the uncombined state exist as diatomic covalent molecules (F₂, Cl₂ etc). These discrete molecules are held together by weak Van der Waals’s forces, which explain the volatile nature of these elements. These elements are also poisonous in nature.
paras.urdu: ہیلوجنز غیر مرکب حالت میں دو ایٹمی اشتراکی سالموں (F₂، Cl₂ وغیرہ) کی صورت میں ہوتے ہیں۔ یہ الگ الگ سالمے کمزور وان ڈر والز قوتوں سے جڑے رہتے ہیں، جو ان عناصر کی فرار پذیر نوعیت کی وضاحت کرتی ہیں۔ یہ عناصر زہریلے بھی ہیں۔
paras.pashto: هالوجنونه په نه ترکیب شوي حالت کې د دوه اټومي کووالنټ مالیکولونو (F₂، Cl₂ او نورو) په بڼه وي. دا جلا مالیکولونه د وان در والس د کمزورو قوو په وسیله سره ساتل کېږي، چې د دې عناصرو د ژر بخار کېدونکي ماهیت تشریح کوي. دا عناصر زهرجن هم دي.

sections.theory:
Halogens in the uncombined state exist as diatomic covalent molecules (F₂, Cl₂ etc). These discrete molecules are held together by weak Van der Waals’s forces, which explain the volatile nature of these elements. These elements are also poisonous in nature.

13.5.1.1 Trend in Atomic Radius

Atomic radii of Group – VII A elements increase down the group as shown in Table 13.25.

Table 13.25 Trend in Atomic Radius in Group –VIIA elements

13.5.1.2 Trend in Electronegativity

Electronegativity of Group–VII A elements decreases gradually from fluorine to iodine down the group as shown below.

Tidbit

Fluorine is the most electronegative element of the periodic table.

Table 13.26 Trend in Electronegativity in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.3 Trend in Electron Affinity

Electron affinity greatly influences the chemical behaviour of atoms by accepting one or more electrons. Electron affinity of an element is defined as “the amount of energy released when an electron is accepted by an atom in the gaseous state to form an anion,” i.e.

Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)     ΔH = −349 kJmol⁻¹

As the energy is released, so electron affinity is given the negative sign. Electron affinity is the measure of the attraction of the nucleus of an atom for the extra electron.

a) Variation in a Group

As we move in a group from top to bottom, there is an increase in the atomic size, nuclear charge and shielding effect. However, the combined effect of increase in atomic size and shielding effect dominates over the effect of increase in the nuclear charge. Hence, force of attraction of the nucleus for the electron to be added decreases resulting in a decrease in electron-affinity values.

However, it has been seen that fluorine has lower electron affinity than chlorine because fluorine has very small size and high charge density which opposes the electron to be added. Electron affinity generally decreases in the following order (I < Br < F < Cl).

Table 13.27 Trend in Electron Affinity in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.4 Trend in Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of Group – VIIA increases down the group due to increase in strength of the Van der Waals forces. This trend is given below.

Table 13.28 Trend in Melting and Boiling Points in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.5 Bond Enthalpies

Bond enthalpy is the amount of heat required to break one mole of covalent bonds to form individual atoms. It begins with the original substance in a gaseous state and ending with gaseous atoms.

Cl–Cl(g) —Δ→ 2Cl(g)

13.5.1.5.1 Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

Bond breaking is an endothermic process and bond enthalpy involved is given positive sign. The bond enthalpies of halogens are given below.

Table 13.29 Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

The abnormal behavior in F–F bond is due to its smaller size and strong repulsion amongst the non-bonded electrons (lone pair) of fluorine atoms. Hence bonds become weak, though bond is short. Thus, enthalpy of fluorine is less than the other halogens.

Halogens in the uncombined state exist as diatomic covalent molecules (F₂, Cl₂ etc). These discrete molecules are held together by weak Van der Waals’s forces, which explain the volatile nature of these elements. These elements are also poisonous in nature.

13.5.1.1 Trend in Atomic Radius

Atomic radii of Group – VII A elements increase down the group as shown in Table 13.25.

Table 13.25 Trend in Atomic Radius in Group –VIIA elements

13.5.1.2 Trend in Electronegativity

Electronegativity of Group–VII A elements decreases gradually from fluorine to iodine down the group as shown below.

Tidbit

Fluorine is the most electronegative element of the periodic table.

Table 13.26 Trend in Electronegativity in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.3 Trend in Electron Affinity

Electron affinity greatly influences the chemical behaviour of atoms by accepting one or more electrons. Electron affinity of an element is defined as “the amount of energy released when an electron is accepted by an atom in the gaseous state to form an anion,” i.e.

Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) ΔH = −349 kJmol⁻¹

As the energy is released, so electron affinity is given the negative sign. Electron affinity is the measure of the attraction of the nucleus of an atom for the extra electron.

a) Variation in a Group

As we move in a group from top to bottom, there is an increase in the atomic size, nuclear charge and shielding effect. However, the combined effect of increase in atomic size and shielding effect dominates over the effect of increase in the nuclear charge. Hence, force of attraction of the nucleus for the electron to be added decreases resulting in a decrease in electron-affinity values.

However, it has been seen that fluorine has lower electron affinity than chlorine because fluorine has very small size and high charge density which opposes the electron to be added. Electron affinity generally decreases in the following order (I < Br < F < Cl).

Table 13.27 Trend in Electron Affinity in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.4 Trend in Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of Group – VIIA increases down the group due to increase in strength of the Van der Waals forces. This trend is given below.

Table 13.28 Trend in Melting and Boiling Points in Group–VIIA Elements

13.5.1.5 Bond Enthalpies

Bond enthalpy is the amount of heat required to break one mole of covalent bonds to form individual atoms. It begins with the original substance in a gaseous state and ending with gaseous atoms.

Cl–Cl(g) —Δ→ 2Cl(g)

13.5.1.5.1 Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

Bond breaking is an endothermic process and bond enthalpy involved is given positive sign. The bond enthalpies of halogens are given below.

Table 13.29 Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

The abnormal behavior in F–F bond is due to its smaller size and strong repulsion amongst the non-bonded electrons (lone pair) of fluorine atoms. Hence bonds become weak, though bond is short. Thus, enthalpy of fluorine is less than the other halogens.
